#### 23.5 Data integrity

| ID | Requirement | Target / rule | How we verify it | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFR-37 | No accepted raw reading is ever lost. | Zero lost readings across the whole test programme, including the power-cut test of NFR-28. | Count readings before and after each destructive test. | [MUST] |
| NFR-38 | Every business action that changes more than one table happens inside one database transaction. Either all of it happens or none of it. | Named transaction boundaries documented for: sample registration, sample acceptance, result submission, verification, report issue, invoice issue, payment receipt, stock issue, state transition. | Code review against the documented list; plus fault-injection test (kill the process mid-action) for the five most important boundaries. | [MUST] |
| NFR-39 | **No partial report can exist.** A report either does not exist, or exists complete with its number, its frozen values, its rendered file, its file fingerprint and its signature record. | No report row without a stored file and fingerprint. A database check enforces this. | Query the reports table for rows failing the rule; must return zero. Repeat after the power-cut test. | [MUST] |
| NFR-40 | Referential integrity is enforced by the database, not only by the application. Every relationship listed in §25 exists as a foreign key. | Zero orphan rows. | Run an orphan-detection script against production monthly; result logged. | [MUST] |
| NFR-41 | Calculated results are reproducible. Re-running the stored calculation on the stored raw readings, using the stored formula version, gives exactly the same reported value including rounding. | 100% match on a regression suite of at least 20 historical worksheets supplied by the laboratory. | Automated regression test, re-run on every release. This is also the software-validation evidence required by ISO/IEC 17025 clause 7.11.2. | [MUST] |
| NFR-42 | Stored report files are tamper-evident. The system can prove a stored report has not changed since issue. | A fingerprint (SHA-256) is stored at issue and re-verified by a scheduled job weekly across all reports. The administrator screen also carries a **"Run integrity check now"** control that re-verifies one report, or all reports, on demand and reports the outcome at once. Any mismatch raises an alert and a Nonconforming Work record, and the file is refused to every requester until the mismatch is closed. | Test: alter one byte of a stored file on disk, run the on-demand check, and confirm the mismatch is reported immediately, the file is refused, an alert is raised and a nonconforming work record opens. The weekly schedule is confirmed separately from the job log (`sys_job_run`). | [MUST] |
| NFR-43 | Nothing in the technical-record chain (samples, readings, results, verifications, reports, audit trail, custody events) can be deleted by the application. | The application's database login has no DELETE permission on those tables. | Attempt a DELETE using the application credentials; must be refused by the database. | [MUST] |
| NFR-44 | Server clocks are correct and synchronised. | All servers and laboratory computers synchronise to the National Informatics Centre time service (`time.nic.in`) or the National Physical Laboratory service. Drift under 1 second. | Check drift on every server monthly; recorded. Required by the CERT-In directions of 28 April 2022. | [MUST] |
| NFR-121 | Adding a trusted timestamp after issue never modifies the issued report file. **Dormant under the OPEN-Q-T31 default, and deliberately kept.** | On the default answer recorded at OPEN-Q-T31 the laboratory needs a valid signature and not long-term validation, so nothing on the present plan applies a timestamp and this rule binds nothing today. It is kept defined rather than deleted, because the day anything does apply one it is the rule that stops an integrity incident. **What brings it back:** the Quality Manager or NABL answering OPEN-Q-T31 the other way in writing; an assessor asking that a report still validate after its signing certificate has expired (M8-47, M21-44); or a Central Silk Board or DigiLocker requirement arriving with the machine-readable report file of Phase 6. **When it binds:** where the timestamp is a detached RFC 3161 token over the signature, it is stored as its own artefact against the signature record (`sys_esign.timestamp_token_ref`). Where an embedded PAdES document timestamp or long-term-validation material is required, the timestamped file is written as a **separate derived attachment** with its own `sys_attachment` row and its own SHA-256, and the frozen issued file is left untouched. The issued file, its `pdf_sha256`, the fingerprint printed on the paper, the fingerprint in the signed QR payload and the fingerprint published by ARC-20 all continue to refer to the issued original, which remains the sole copy the ARC-21 browser file-check compares against. Applying a timestamp is logged as an event on the report. | While dormant, the standing check is that no code path writes to a stored issued file at all, which the weekly job of NFR-42 already proves. When it binds: issue a report with the internet disconnected; reconnect; confirm the weekly integrity job of NFR-42 passes, no Nonconforming Work record opens, and the customer's original copy still matches in the browser file-check. | [MUST] |

No password appears in any log, error message or backup in readable form. | Inspect the user table and the logs; search backups for known test passwords. | [MUST] |
| NFR-47 | **No shared or generic logins.** Every person has their own named account. | Zero shared accounts. Account names are traceable to a person in the personnel register. Sharing is prohibited in writing and the system displays the logged-in user's name on every screen. This prohibition governs human logins. The single scheduler service account of DB-05 is not a shared human login: no person may authenticate as it. | Account list reviewed and signed by the Unit Incharge before go-live and every six months; the review lists service accounts separately and confirms there is exactly one and that it has no interactive credential. | [MUST] |
| NFR-48 | Password policy: minimum 10 characters, checked against a list of common passwords, no forced periodic rotation, forced change on first login and after an administrator reset. | Enforced by the system. | Attempt to set "password123"; must be refused. | [MUST] |
| NFR-49 | Accounts lock after 8 failed login attempts for 15 minutes, and every failure is logged with the source address. | Enforced and logged. | Test 9 failed logins. | [MUST] |
| NFR-50 | A second factor (one-time code by SMS, or an authenticator application) is required for accounts that can authorise reports, change master data, or administer the system. | Enforced for the roles Unit Incharge, Quality Manager and Administrator. | Test each role. | [SHOULD] |
| NFR-51 | Sessions expire after 60 minutes of inactivity, or 15 minutes for administrator sessions. Logging out invalidates the session on the server. | Enforced. | Timed test. | [MUST] |
| NFR-52 | Attachments (sample photographs, calibration certificates, signature images, report files) are encrypted at rest. | Whole-disk encryption on the server plus operating-system file permissions restricting access to the application account. Signature images are additionally encrypted at the file level with a key held outside the database. | Inspect a raw disk image or a stolen backup file and confirm attachments are not readable. | [MUST] |
| NFR-53 | Secrets (database password, signing key passphrase, SMS gateway key, bank credentials) are never in source control, never in a file committed to the repository, and never printed in logs or error pages. | Zero secrets in the repository history, checked by an automated scanner in the build. | Run a secret scanner over the full Git history before go-live; result attached to the release record. | [MUST] |
| NFR-54 | Dependencies are patched. | A dependency vulnerability scan runs on every build and at least monthly. Critical and high-severity issues in components reachable from the internet are fixed within 14 days; others within 90 days. A record of each decision is kept. | Scan report per release, filed with the change record. | [MUST] |
| NFR-55 | A security review is completed before go-live and before the public verification service is exposed to the internet. | Covers, at minimum: authentication and session handling, access control on every endpoint (including the "can a tester read a customer name by calling the interface directly" test), injection, file-upload handling, the public verification endpoint, rate limiting, and secrets handling. Findings are recorded with a fix or an accepted-risk note signed by the Unit Incharge. | Written review report. For a Government domain, a "safe to host" certificate from a CERT-In empanelled auditor is likely to be required; see OPEN-Q-T3. | [MUST] |
| NFR-56 | Uploaded files are restricted by type and size, stored outside the web-served directory, renamed on storage, and never executed. | Allowed: JPEG, PNG, PDF. Maximum 10 MB per file. | Attempt to upload an executable and a very large file. | [MUST] |
| NFR-57 | System logs are retained for 180 rolling days, stored in India, and available to CERT-In on request, as required by the direction of 28 April 2022. **Personal data (names, telephone numbers, addresses) is scrubbed from application logs** so the mandatory log store does not itself become a data-protection problem. | 180 days retained; a documented log-content rule; a sample of 100 log lines contains no personal data. | Inspect logs and count retention days. | [MUST] |
| NFR-58 | Access to customer identity and to commercial data is enforced at the data layer, not by hiding fields in the screen. A tester calling the interface directly must not receive the customer name. | The response sent to a tester's browser physically does not contain the customer name, address, telephone number, tax registration number or price. | Inspect the raw network response on the tester's result-entry screen with browser developer tools. This is test AC-07. | [MUST] |

#### 23.8 Accessibility and Government website guidelines

| ID | Requirement | Target / rule | How we verify it | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFR-68 | The **public report-verification page** conforms to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA, as harmonised by the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites and Apps (GIGW) 3.0. | Zero Level AA failures on the page. Specifically: semantic headings in order; visible keyboard focus; text contrast at least 4.5 to 1; a real label on the file-check control; full keyboard operation; page language declared. | Automated accessibility scan plus a manual keyboard-and-screen-reader walkthrough. Recorded. | [MUST] |
| NFR-69 | The verification result is never conveyed by colour alone. The banner carries an icon and the words GENUINE — VALID, GENUINE — SUPERSEDED, GENUINE — WITHDRAWN or NOT GENUINE, exactly as enumerated in M9-14. No other banner wording is permitted. | Readable in greyscale. | Print the page in black and white; confirm the wording matches the four M9-14 states exactly. | [MUST] |
| NFR-70 | Report PDFs are generated as **tagged PDFs with a real text layer, logical reading order and labelled table structure**. A scanned image of a printed page is not acceptable output. **Rendering correctly is not enough — the text has to be recoverable.** Whatever is printed on the page must come back out of the finished file as the same characters in the same logical order, with nothing dropped. For Indic scripts that takes two mechanisms, and neither one replaces the other: (a) the ToUnicode map is built from the shaper's record of which original characters each cluster came from, not from the order the glyphs were drawn in; and (b) every Indic run is additionally wrapped in a marked-content span carrying its logical string as /ActualText, encoded UTF-16BE with a byte-order mark, which a conforming reader prefers over ToUnicode. Why both are needed, and why neither may be dropped as redundant, is set out in ARC-47 in §24.4. | Text is selectable and searchable in the PDF; tags present. **Extraction is exact**: every string written into the document is found again, character for character and in logical order, in the text extracted back out of the finished file — no dropped viramas, no reordering, no substitutions. Passing a validator is not evidence of this. veraPDF passes a file whose text layer is in visual order, and no accessibility validator detects the defect, so the check has to be written by hand. | Automated, in the build, not by eye: extract the text from the generated file and compare it against the strings that were written, failing the build on any difference. Then open the PDF, select and copy a Telugu and a Devanagari line and paste them into a plain text editor. Then run formal PDF/UA-1 validation with veraPDF, profile ua1, over the **signed** file and not only the unsigned one, because signing appends to the file and the signed file is the only one anybody receives. **The PDF library and the text shaper are decided on this basis before Phase 1 coding** — §24.4 records what was tested and PLN-28 is the test that holds it there, now measured in both states rather than assumed. | [MUST] |
| NFR-71 | The internal staff application meets a reduced but stated accessibility baseline: full keyboard operation, visible focus, 4.5 to 1 text contrast, minimum 14-pixel body text, and no information conveyed by colour alone. | Baseline met on all screens. | Manual checklist. | [SHOULD] |
| NFR-72 | The public verification page is kept deliberately small — one page, one status banner, one small table, one file-check control — so that it can be made and kept conformant cheaply. | Page weight under 200 kilobytes excluding the QR image; no external fonts; no third-party analytics. | Measure page weight. | [MUST] |

**OPEN-Q-T3:** Will the public verification page sit on a `gov.in`, `nic.in` or `res.in` domain, and does Central Silk Board require STQC "Certified Quality Website" certification and a CERT-In empanelled auditor's "safe to host" certificate before it goes live? — *Recommended default:* assume "safe to host" is required and budget 6 weeks of lead time; build the page to GIGW 3.0 from day one so certification is a review, not a rebuild; do not let this block the internal system going live.

The shaper is part of the recorded configuration, not a preference; see §24.4. | Correct rendering tested with at least 20 real Telugu names and addresses, **and every one of those 20 strings extracted back out of the file and compared character for character with what was written**. The test runs against the fonts actually shipped — the vendored Noto Sans Telugu and Noto Sans Devanagari named in ARC-48. **Substituting a font invalidates the result**: shaping defects are font-dependent, and the crash above reproduces against those faces and does not reproduce against the Telugu faces that ship with macOS. | Print and inspect, **and** run the automated extraction comparison NFR-70 requires over the same 20 strings. **Test this in Phase 0 or Phase 1, not at the end — the PDF font stack is hard to change late.** Changing a font is a change under ARC-48. | [MUST] |
| NFR-94 | Dates display as DD-MM-YYYY. Numbers use the Indian digit grouping convention for money (for example 7,56,789) and plain grouping for measurements. #### 23.12 Backup and recovery

| ID | Requirement | Target | How we verify it | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFR-95 | **Recovery Point Objective (RPO) — how much work we can afford to lose: 15 minutes for the database and for the file store of issued controlled documents (report PDFs, signed invoices, receipts, credit notes); 24 hours for all other attachments.** | Continuous database transaction-log archiving to the dedicated local backup disk, with a copy taken at least every 15 minutes; issued controlled-document files copied to the same disk at issue (NFR-97). | Restore test: confirm no more than 15 minutes of transactions lost, and that an issued report file created in the last 15 minutes before the failure is present and matches its stored fingerprint. | [MUST] |
| NFR-96 | **Recovery Time Objective (RTO) — how long the lab can be down: 4 working hours** for a software or data failure; **1 working day** for total loss of the server hardware. | Achieved with the documented restore procedure. | Timed restore drill. | [MUST] |
| NFR-97 | Backup schedule: a full database backup every night; transaction logs every 15 minutes; **issued controlled-document files (report PDFs, signed invoices, receipts, credit notes) are copied to the local backup disk as part of the business action that issues them, and the issue is not confirmed until that copy exists and its SHA-256 matches the stored fingerprint — this copy is to a local disk only, never a synchronous off-site upload, so that §24.1's rule and NFR-16's 5-second budget still hold**; all other attachments backed up nightly (changed files only); a monthly full backup retained for 12 months; a yearly full backup retained for 7 years. | Schedule automated and monitored; a failed backup raises an alert the same day. | Backup log reviewed weekly; and one issued report checked on the backup disk within a minute of issue. | [MUST] |
| NFR-98 | Backup copies: one on a **third, separate, non-mirrored internal disk dedicated to backups** (the mirror in NFR-116 is a single logical volume and therefore is not a second copy); one on an external disk **swapped weekly and kept off the premises**; one encrypted copy uploaded off-site when the internet allows. | Three copies, at least one off-site, all encrypted. | Inspect the media; confirm encryption by attempting to read without the key. | [MUST] |
| NFR-99 | **A restore test is performed monthly onto the staging environment and the result is recorded and signed.** An untested backup does not count as a backup. | 12 recorded restore tests per year. | The restore-test log. | [MUST] |
| NFR-100 | The restore procedure is written as a step-by-step document that a person who did not build the system can follow, and is stored on paper in the laboratory as well as electronically. | Document exists; a second person completes a restore following only the document. | Have someone other than the developer perform one restore drill. | [MUST] |
| NFR-101 | Backups never contain readable secrets, and production data is never restored into the development environment without personal data being replaced. | Verified by inspection. | Inspect a backup and the development database. | [MUST] |

#### 23.13 Auditability

| ID | Requirement | Target / rule | How we verify it | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NFR-102 | Every change to a raw reading, a result, a method, an equipment status, a personnel authorisation, a rate, a report or a numbered document records: what changed, the old value, the new value, who changed it, the exact time, and a **reason that cannot be left blank**. | 100% coverage of the listed entities. Reason mandatory for those changes. | Change one value of each type and inspect the audit trail; then attempt a change with a blank reason and confirm refusal. | [MUST] |
| NFR-103 | The audit trail is written by the database itself, so that a change made directly in the database by any means is still recorded. | Database triggers, not only application code. | Make a change with a direct database statement and confirm it appears in the audit trail. This is test AC-42. | [MUST] |
| NFR-104 | The original value is **visible in the screen**, not merely recoverable from a backup. Any changed field shows a "changed — view history" indicator, and the history view shows the whole chain, original first. | Present on result, report and equipment screens. | UAT check. | [MUST] |
| NFR-105 | Audit rows cannot be changed or deleted by the application, and are never removed by a retention purge while the record they describe is still retained. | The application's database account holds INSERT and SELECT on the audit tables and nothing else. **UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, ALTER and DROP are revoked, as is the right to create, alter, disable or drop a trigger on them**, and the audit tables are owned by a separate database account the application cannot authenticate as — the full revoked list of M21-31. A guard trigger raises an error on every operation a trigger can intercept and records the attempt as an audit row naming the account; the remainder are stopped by the grant model and the table ownership, and the refusal reaches the daily health digest through the database error log (ARC-35). Every audit row carries a per-row SHA-256 chain value, so a row altered or removed by any route breaks the chain. | Attempt each revoked operation in turn as the application login; every one must be refused and the attempt must be visible. Then run the chain re-computation of M21-31b over the whole table and confirm it verifies; then alter one row as the owning account and confirm the re-computation reports the break and names the row. | [MUST] |
| NFR-106 | For any sample, an authorised person can print a single page showing the complete history: receipt, custody movements, allocations, readings with their equipment and reagent lots, changes with reasons, verification, report issue, amendments, and disposal. | One-click "sample history" printout. | Print it for a sample that has been amended. | [MUST] |
| NFR-107 | The system can answer "as at this date, who was authorised for this method?" and "as at this date, what price applied to this test?" | Both are queries against dated records, not reconstructions. | Run both queries for a date two years in the past on the test dataset. | [MUST] |
| NFR-108 | A certificate can be produced for any report, stating the system that produced it, the period the system has been in regular use, the source data, and the integrity controls — the statement needed under section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (previously section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act) if a report is ever produced in a dispute. | Generated on demand for any report. | Generate one. | [SHOULD] |

### 24. Recommended architecture and technology

#### 24.1 The single most important architectural rule

> **The application must run completely and correctly on one ordinary server inside the laboratory, with no internet connection, for at least a full working week.** Every feature that needs the outside world — the public verification page, payment reconciliation, Invoice Reference Number requests, SMS, off-site backup — is an optional, queued, retryable outbound job. None of them may sit on the path a scientist takes to log a sample, enter a reading, or issue a report.

Everything below follows from that rule and from the site facts: the unit is next to the Government Cocoon Market at Regatipalli, it serves walk-in customers with same-day expectations, and district connectivity and power are not dependable.

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-01 | The complete internal system runs on a single server inside the laboratory, with no dependency on any external service for its core function. | [MUST] |
| ARC-02 | Every outbound integration is implemented as a queued job with retry, a visible queue and a manual retry, per NFR-31. | [MUST] |
| ARC-03 | The public verification service is a physically separate, minimal, internet-facing component with read-only data, per ARC-18 to ARC-22. | [MUST] |
| ARC-04 | Nothing in the design prevents a later move to a Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) empanelled cloud in an Indian region, or to National Informatics Centre hosting. No feature depends on a service that only one vendor offers. | [MUST] |

#### 24.2 Deployment model — comparison and recommendation

| | On-premise server at the unit | Cloud only | **Hybrid: local server plus a small cloud verification service (recommended)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Works when internet is down | Yes, fully | **No — the laboratory stops** | Yes, fully, for all internal work |
| Public QR verification works when the unit's power is off | No | Yes | **Yes** |
| Purchase route | One-time capital purchase; a unit head can plausibly get this sanctioned | Recurring subscription; must be from a MeitY-empanelled provider registered on the Government e-Marketplace, needs an annual budget line | One-time server plus a very small recurring cost for one small internet host |
| Data location | In the laboratory, in Central Silk Board custody | In an Indian region of an empanelled provider; must be verified per service, not per provider | Records in the laboratory; only public verification records outside |
| Who fixes the hardware | The unit, with no on-site information-technology support | The provider | The unit for the server; the provider for the small public host |
| Risk if the single server dies | Highest — mitigated by disk mirroring, tested backups and a documented 1-day rebuild | Low | Same as on-premise for internal work; verification unaffected |
| Ongoing cost | Lowest | Highest and recurring | Low, with a small recurring element |
| Complexity for a solo developer | Lowest | Medium | Low-to-medium; one extra small deployment |
| Data-protection position | Easiest to defend | Needs a written agreement covering confidentiality, data location, breach notification, sub-processors and exit, plus a supplier evaluation record | Easiest for records; the public component holds only non-identifying data |

**Recommendation: the hybrid.** The internal laboratory system on one server in the building; a separate, tiny, hardened internet-facing verification service; an outbound queue between them. This is the only option that satisfies both "the laboratory must not stop when the line drops" and "a buyer with a paper certificate must be able to check it".

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-05 | Deployment is hybrid as described above. The internal server holds all records; the public verification service holds only a published verification record per issued report. | [MUST] |
| ARC-06 | The internal server runs on Linux (recommended) or Windows Server, in a documented configuration, with the operating system, database and runtime versions recorded, because deviating from the recorded configuration is a change requiring the control of NFR-114. | [MUST] |
| ARC-07 | Wired Ethernet to the server and to the label printer. Wireless only for tablets. This removes a whole class of intermittent faults. | [SHOULD] |

#### 24.3 Application shape

| ID | Requirement | Reason | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| ARC-08 | One web application, accessed by a browser on the laboratory network. No installed client software on staff computers. | A shared low-specification desktop cannot be relied on to have anything installed; and a browser-only client means a new machine works immediately. | [MUST] |
| ARC-09 | **Server-rendered pages with selective interactivity**, not a full single-page application. Only the screens that need it — result-entry grids, batch registration, allocation boards — carry rich in-page behaviour. | A server-rendered application is faster on 4 GB machines and slow links, is far simpler for one developer to maintain over years, degrades gracefully, and avoids shipping a large program to the browser. | [MUST] |
| ARC-10 | The interface is responsive so the customer portal and the public verification page work on a phone. **No native mobile application in version 1.** | A native application means two codebases, an app-store account and a release process the unit cannot sustain. | [MUST] |
| ARC-11 | Business rules live on the server, never only in the browser. Access control, state transitions, calculations, number allocation and validation are all re-checked on the server. | A rule enforced only in the screen is not a rule. | [MUST] |
| ARC-12 | The application is organised as clearly separated modules with one service class per business action, and exactly **one** function that executes state transitions. | State logic scattered across screens is the most common source of impossible data in laboratory systems. | [MUST] |

#### 24.4 Technology stack

**These recommendations apply as written, and the two that mattered most are now decisions rather than recommendations.** The laboratory system is a standalone application, not a layer inside somebody else's package, so there is no existing language, framework or database it has to inherit. ARC-13 and ARC-14 record the two branches and which of them is operative. Decision 1, the stack, is stated immediately below. Decision 2, what the signature on a report has to achieve, is registered as an open question with a recommended default at OPEN-Q-T31, and this section builds to that default and states what it costs if the default is wrong.

**Decision 1 — the stack is Node.js with TypeScript, server-rendered, on PostgreSQL 16.** What decided it is this section's own rule: *anything the developer has not shipped before: reject*. One person maintains this system for years, in a district unit with no information-technology support, and the developer has shipped JavaScript and Node work and nothing else. A framework he would be learning on the job is a larger risk than any difference in library quality between the candidates — and larger than the one genuine weakness this choice carries, which is set out in the digital-signing row. The earlier text of this section left the language open and offered three frameworks the developer does not use; that is now closed. Everything downstream of the choice — the PDF and signing rows especially — was then built and tested rather than assumed, because a stack chosen for maintainability still has to be able to produce the document this laboratory issues.

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-13 | **Not operative.** This rule provided for the case where the laboratory layer had to be built inside an existing accounting system — sharing its database, its login, its screens or its deployment — in which case that system's language, framework and database would have decided the stack, and this section's recommendations would have been overridden except for the PDF, signing and verification components. No such system exists at this unit, so the case does not arise and ARC-14 is the operative branch. The rule is kept, with its reasoning, because it becomes live again the moment anyone proposes housing this system inside another: if that is ever proposed, the stack question is reopened, answered in writing, and recorded in the ARC-06 configuration record **before** any code is written against it. | [MUST] |
| ARC-14 | **Operative.** The laboratory layer is a separate, standalone application. It owns its customer master, its numbering series, its invoices and receipts and its stock records outright, and the recommendations below apply in full. If an external accounting system is ever introduced — the unit acquires one, or Central Silk Board mandates one — it is joined by a documented interface with **one system of record per field**, never two editable copies of the customer address, and the laboratory system must still run with that interface switched off (M22-17). | [MUST] |

| Concern | Recommendation | Deciding reason | Honest alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Language and framework | **Node.js on a long-term-support release (24 LTS at the time of writing), with TypeScript, server-rendered.** Server-side templates producing HTML, with selective in-page interactivity only where ARC-09 requires it. The exact runtime version is recorded in the ARC-06 configuration record and moves only along a long-term-support line. | The deciding factor is not language quality; it is that **one person must maintain this for years and a government unit must be able to find a replacement developer in India.** This section's own rule settles it: anything the developer has not shipped before is rejected, and the developer has shipped JavaScript and Node work only. JavaScript is also the language in which a replacement is easiest to find in an Indian district town. The cost is real and is not hidden here: of the four candidates Node has the weakest PDF signing libraries, which is exactly why the PDF and signing rows below are written to a position that was built and validated rather than to a hope. | PHP 8.3 with Laravel, .NET 8 with ASP.NET Core, Python with Django: all three are sound, all three have stronger document libraries, and all three would be a first project for this developer. **Rejected on that ground, not on merit.** A second runtime used only for documents is a different question, and is answered in the PDF row. Anything the developer has not shipped before: reject. |
| Relational database | **PostgreSQL 16.** There is no other application whose database this one has to match, so the choice is made on merit. Reached from Node through the standard `pg` driver with explicit SQL and hand-written, numbered migrations (ARC-29). No tool that hides the schema, because in this system the constraints and triggers of §25 *are* the design. | PostgreSQL gives stronger constraint checking, proper timestamp-with-timezone handling, and trigger support, which the audit trail in §25 depends on, and it makes the trigger-written audit log of DB-04 and the revoked grants of NFR-105 straightforward. The counter-argument for matching another product's database — one engine to look after rather than two, which matters in a unit with no information-technology support — assumed this system would be built inside an existing package. It is not (ARC-14). The Node decision does not weigh here either way: the concurrency behaviour the number-allocation rule needs is the database's, not the language's. | MariaDB or MySQL 8: workable, and the right choice if the developer is markedly stronger there, but the constraint and trigger work of §25 costs more effort. SQL Server: fine technically, licensing cost is the problem. **SQLite: reject** — it does not give the concurrent-write behaviour the number-allocation rule needs. **Any non-relational database: reject** — this data is deeply relational and must be queryable by an auditor. |
| Background job runner | A **database-backed** queue table in the same PostgreSQL database, claimed with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, drained by a single worker process supervised by the operating system. | A database-backed queue means one fewer service to install, monitor and back up on a machine nobody administers, and it puts the queue inside the same backup — and the same transaction — as the work that enqueued it. Volumes here are tiny. Node brings no queue of its own to inherit, so this is written rather than configured: a couple of hundred lines, and worth them. | A Redis-backed queue (BullMQ or similar): faster, one more service to keep alive. Reject for this deployment. |
| Scheduled jobs | The operating system scheduler calling one entry point, which then dispatches all due tasks. | One scheduled entry, not fifteen, so there is one place to check when something did not run. | Framework scheduler: same thing; keep one entry point either way. |
| PDF generation | **pdfkit 0.19.1, with harfbuzzjs 1.6.0 replacing fontkit as the text shaper**, driven from the dedicated document component of ARC-17. This position was built and validated, not read about: a report-shaped document — embedded font, a heading, a tagged table with header cells and scope, a paragraph running across a page break, a figure with alternative text, artifact-marked page furniture, and a digital signature applied afterwards — passes formal PDF/UA-1 validation, veraPDF 1.30.2, profile ua1, 106 of 106 rules. Tables stay tagged across page breaks, and signing does not disturb the structure tree. Three conditions come with it, all of them written into ARC-17 as build rules: the structure tree is **hand-built**, because no library on this stack infers tags from layout; every Indic run carries its logical string as marked-content `/ActualText`; and the spurious character-set entry pdfkit emits when the accessibility subset is requested is stripped after rendering. Stock fontkit is replaced outright rather than patched: it throws an uncaught type error on ordinary Telugu words, including ప్రయోగశాల (laboratory), its Indic shaping engine was last functionally touched in 2017, and its repository has had no commits since August 2024. harfbuzzjs is the HarfBuzz project's own build — pure WebAssembly, no dependencies, about 1.2 MB, nothing to compile on the laboratory server, behind roughly sixty lines of pdfkit layout override — which is what lets it vendor cleanly offline for ARC-16. PLN-28 is the test that holds all of this in place. | This is the one place where library capability, not developer preference, decides, so it was tested rather than argued. Tagged PDF for the accessibility requirement of NFR-70, a valid certificate-based signature, and correct Telugu and Devanagari shaping (NFR-93) are needed together, and the common belief that Node cannot do the first is wrong — it can, and the evidence is a validator run that ARC-30 repeats on every push. What Node genuinely cannot do is long-term validation, which is the signing row's subject and OPEN-Q-T31's. A second runtime purely for document generation remains a last resort: if one becomes unavoidable it is recorded as an explicit exception in the ARC-06 configuration record with its own ARC-16 offline vendoring plan, because a district unit with no information-technology support must patch and rebuild only one dependency tree. Rendering a web page to an image is **not acceptable output**. | **ReportLab with pyHanko on Python: withdrawn as false — see the correction below this table.** What Python does give is pyHanko, the strongest signing library on any stack and the escape hatch named in the signing row; tagged output there means either a commercial ReportLab PLUS licence, which is a cost and an ARC-46 licence question, or a different generator — and a second runtime either way. Java or .NET: iText 8 and Apache PDFBox produce tagged PDF and full PAdES on their own account, not verified here, but iText's default terms are the copyleft network licence ARC-46 forbids without a commercial licence bought in Central Silk Board's name, and both are stacks this developer has not shipped. HTML-to-PDF converters (wkhtmltopdf, Puppeteer): easy layout, weak or absent tagging and signing. Acceptable only for internal working documents, never for issued reports. |
| Digital signing of PDFs | **@signpdf/signpdf 3.x with the `@signpdf/placeholder-plain` placeholder**, applied to the rendered file inside the document component, behind an interface with three interchangeable implementations: a local key file (development only), a hardware security module holding an organisational Document Signer certificate, and a remote signing service **whose signing key remains inside the laboratory network**. Two build rules, both established by test rather than by documentation: the signature is applied **invisibly**, and the visible "Digitally signed by ..." block is drawn as ordinary tagged page content, because a visible signature widget fails PDF/UA on two counts — the widget is not nested in a form structure element, and it carries no alternative description — and nothing on this stack fixes that; and `@signpdf/placeholder-pdfkit`, the placeholder that looks like the obvious choice here, is **never** used, because its peer dependency is pinned to pdfkit ^0.11 against the 0.19.1 this uses and it fails **silently**, emitting no output at all. An electronic-signature service provider reached across the internet is **not** an option on the report-issue path, because M8-46 and NFR-32 forbid any call outside the laboratory network there; such a provider may be used for non-report documents only, and if one is adopted for that purpose it is recorded as a fourth implementation restricted to those documents. | Making this an interface from day one means the signing decision (§ Signature module) can change without touching the report generator — which is exactly the insurance OPEN-Q-T31 needs. This library reaches a basic valid signature, the PAdES B-B profile, which is what OPEN-Q-T31's default records as the requirement, and a signed report is still a conformant tagged PDF afterwards. It cannot reach the timestamped or long-term profiles, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of effort: the underlying cryptography library hardcodes three signed-attribute identifiers, emits a malformed structure for a fourth **without raising an error**, and hardcodes the unsigned attributes — where a signature timestamp has to live — as empty, with no public way in. A library that fails silently is worse than one that refuses, which is why both of these are written down here rather than left to be discovered. | pyHanko on Python: reaches every PAdES profile up to B-LTA, and is the named escape hatch if OPEN-Q-T31 is answered the other way — invoked as a command line off the report-issue path, with its second runtime recorded as an ARC-06 exception. A commercial Java or .NET library: also complete, also unshipped by this developer, also an ARC-46 licence question. None of them changes the interface: build it regardless of which implementation is chosen first. |
| Barcode and QR generation | A well-used open-source library producing QR Code (ISO/IEC 18004) at error-correction level M, plus Code 128 for the secondary one-dimensional barcode. | QR is readable by any staff phone and by a ₹2,000 imaging scanner, and the laboratory is already committing to QR on reports, so there is one mental model. | Data Matrix: technically denser, choose it only if labelling items under 15 mm. |
| Label printing | Raw printer commands (ZPL or EPL) sent over the network to the label printer, generated by the application. | Removes the Windows print driver entirely, which is the single most common failure point in a small laboratory system. | Windows driver printing: reject for labels. |
| Attachment storage | Files on the server's own filesystem in a dated directory structure, with all metadata in a database table. Move to S3-compatible object storage later if needed, behind the same interface. | Simplest thing that survives a restore; and the interface means the move is configuration. See DB-14 for why files are never stored inside database rows. | Object storage from day one: more moving parts than a single-server unit needs. |
| Email | An Indian provider or the unit's existing government mail relay, called from the outbound queue. | Data stays in India; and it must not be on the critical path. | Any provider that stores message content outside India: reject. |
| SMS | An Indian SMS gateway, with the template registration that Indian telecommunications rules require. Messages carry no personal data beyond what the recipient already knows. | A reeler in Dharmavaram is far more likely to read an SMS than an email. | WhatsApp business messaging: attractive, more approval overhead; treat as a later phase. |
| Search | Ordinary database indexes and, if needed, the database's built-in text search. | At the volumes in §23.0, a separate search engine is unnecessary complexity. | A dedicated search service: reject for this scale. |
| Reporting and analytics | Built-in screens plus CSV and Excel export. No separate reporting tool. | The monthly return to CSTRI headquarters must be one click inside the system; a separate tool guarantees a parallel spreadsheet. | A business-intelligence tool: later, and only if headquarters asks. |

**A correction, recorded against ARC-17.** Until this revision the PDF row above named **ReportLab with pyHanko on Python** as a pair meeting all three requirements. That recommendation is **withdrawn, because it was false.** Open-source ReportLab cannot produce tagged PDF at all: structure elements, structure-parent references, alternative text and marked-content emission are absent from its source, and automatic tagging is a feature of the commercial ReportLab PLUS product. Anyone who followed the recommendation would have discovered this after committing the document component to Python. What is true instead: pyHanko is an excellent signing library, ReportLab is a good generator of untagged PDF, and the pair does not satisfy NFR-70. It is recorded here rather than quietly edited away, because ARC-17 exists so that a wrong library choice costs one component instead of the whole system, and because a reader who was told something false is entitled to see it named.

**What it costs if OPEN-Q-T31 is answered the other way.** The rows above are built to that question's recommended default — a valid signature, not long-term validation — on the strength of a verbal answer from the Unit Incharge, which is recorded there as an assumption and not as a fact. If the written answer from the Quality Manager or NABL turns out to require long-term validation, the remedy is not a code change but a change of component: the signing implementation is replaced through the ARC-17 interface with pyHanko run as a command line off the report-issue path, its second runtime recorded as an ARC-06 exception with its own ARC-16 vendoring plan. Budget two to three developer-weeks, and a second dependency tree to patch for the life of the system. Nothing already issued becomes invalid: NFR-121 governs how the material is added afterwards, to a separate derived file, without altering one byte of the original. This is cheap to prevent and awkward to repair, so the written answer is a Phase 0 task (PLN-04, PLN-06), not a Phase 6 one.

**Why long-term validation could not sit on the report-issue path in any language.** Worth stating once here, where the technology is chosen, so that it is not later mistaken for a limitation of this stack. Long-term validation needs revocation evidence fetched from the certifying authority — an online certificate status response or a revocation list — and an RFC 3161 round trip to a timestamping authority. Both are calls outside the laboratory network, and M8-46 and NFR-32 forbid such a call on the path that issues a report, because a report must issue with the line down. So even on a stack whose libraries do it comfortably, long-term validation is applied **after** issue, from the outbound queue, under NFR-121. The language decides how that material gets applied, never whether it may sit on the issue path.

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-15 | Avoid any architecture that only works on one vendor's proprietary managed service. This application may have to move from a laptop, to a unit server, to National Informatics Centre hosting, to an empanelled cloud, possibly more than once, because of decisions taken above the Unit Incharge's level. | [MUST] |
| ARC-16 | No build step or run-time behaviour requires the internet. All dependencies are vendored or cached so the application can be rebuilt and redeployed with the line down. This bites hardest on the document component, and it is one of the reasons for the choices in §24.4: the text shaper is a self-contained WebAssembly build of about 1.2 MB, with no dependencies and nothing to compile on the laboratory server. Any replacement that needs a compiler toolchain, a system library or a download at install time fails this rule, whatever its other merits. | [MUST] |
| ARC-17 | The document component (render, tag, sign, hash) is a separate, replaceable part with a defined input and output, so that a change of PDF library does not touch the rest of the system. Four rules govern how it is written, each a consequence of what §24.4 records as tested: (a) the structure tree is **hand-built** as the document is laid out, because no library on this stack infers tags from layout — so the layout layer is written tag-first from the first template, and cannot be retrofitted afterwards without rewriting it; (b) every Telugu, Devanagari or other Indic run is emitted inside a marked-content span carrying the **logical** string as its `/ActualText`, because the text layer is otherwise written in visual order, which leaves the certificate unsearchable, uncopyable and read aloud in the wrong character order — the substance of NFR-70, not a cosmetic detail, and something no accessibility validator detects; (c) the spurious character-set entry emitted for the accessibility subset is stripped after rendering, because the format does not require it and it fails validation for some fonts while passing for others, so the build looks healthy until somebody changes the typeface; and (d) signing is invisible, with the visible signature block drawn as tagged page content. PLN-28 is the test that enforces all four. Replaceability here is not housekeeping: it is what makes the OPEN-Q-T31 default survivable if the written answer goes the other way. | [MUST] |
| ARC-46 | Every third-party library's licence is recorded in the technical manual and must be compatible with NFR-113's handover of the source code to Central Silk Board as its property. A library offered under a copyleft network licence is permitted only if a commercial licence is purchased in Central Silk Board's name; the default terms of some widely used PDF libraries conflict with that handover, so the licence is checked before the library is chosen, not after. | [MUST] |
| ARC-47 | **Text recovery from an issued document rests on two mechanisms and both are mandatory; neither is a substitute for the other.** (a) The shaping engine attributes each cluster's original code points to the first glyph of that cluster, so the `/ToUnicode` map is built from logical order instead of from the glyph order that shaping produces. This was checked in the emitted map rather than assumed: `<0c1f 0c4d 0c1f 0c41>` for the whole ట్టు cluster, `<0930 094d 0921>` for the र ् ड of बोर्ड, which keeps its virama. (b) Every Indic run is additionally wrapped in a marked-content span carrying `/ActualText` holding the logical string, encoded UTF-16BE with a byte-order mark — the span ARC-17(b) requires — because a conforming reader prefers `/ActualText` over `/ToUnicode`. **Why both, stated plainly because it is the kind of thing a later developer will otherwise simplify away:** `/ToUnicode` maps a glyph to a string, so a glyph that begins two different clusters can carry only one mapping, and in శ్రీ ధర్మవరం the glyph ర begins both ర్మ and రం — one of the two is unavoidably lost. That is a structural limit of the PDF format, not a defect in the shaping engine, and it is exactly why `/ActualText` is the authoritative mechanism. Measured with (a) absent, the library as shipped extracts बोर्ड as बोरड with the virama silently dropped, पट्टु as पटु्ट and मूर्ति as मूरि्त, leaving the certificate unsearchable, uncopyable and read aloud in the wrong character order — the substance of NFR-70 and NFR-93, not a cosmetic detail. veraPDF passes a file carrying this defect and no accessibility validator detects it, so PLN-28's character-for-character comparison of the extracted text against the strings that went in is the only check that will. | [MUST] |
| ARC-48 | The faces used by the document component are **Noto Sans, Noto Sans Telugu and Noto Sans Devanagari, all three under the SIL Open Font License 1.1**, held in the repository beside the code with their `OFL.txt`. The Latin face belongs in that list for a reason that is easy to miss and was found by measurement: ARC-52 rules out the standard fonts a PDF library offers by default, because they cannot be embedded, so the English text, the numerals and the punctuation on a certificate need a vendored face exactly as the Telugu and the Devanagari do. The three were chosen on two grounds that are requirements rather than taste: the licence is compatible with handing the source and its assets to Central Silk Board as its property (ARC-46), and the files vendor cleanly with nothing to fetch or compile at install time (ARC-16). **The fonts are part of the configuration recorded under ARC-06, not interchangeable assets.** The shaping failure recorded in §24.4 reproduces against these faces and does **not** reproduce against the Telugu faces that ship with macOS, and the subset defect of ARC-49 failed for one Telugu face while others passed. Every result in §24.4, and every pass of PLN-28, is therefore a statement about named font files. Substituting or upgrading a face is a change under NFR-114 that requires PLN-28 to be re-run and its shaping golden file regenerated before the change is accepted; a report template must never fall back to whatever face the server happens to have installed. | [MUST] |
| ARC-49 | **A known defect in a third-party library, recorded with a named workaround so that it is not rediscovered.** Asking pdfkit 0.19.1 for the accessibility subset sets an internal flag that its font code reads as a request for the archival subset, so it emits a `/CIDSet` built only from the glyphs actually drawn while the subsetter writes the further glyphs those glyphs depend on. The two disagree and veraPDF then fails rule 7.21.4.2-2. The failure is **font-dependent** — one Telugu face failed with 23 glyphs in the subset and only 15 marked in the set, other faces passed — which is why ARC-48 fixes the font, and why the build looks healthy until somebody changes it. `/CIDSet` is not required by PDF/UA at all; it is required only by the archival profile that flag belongs to. The workaround is the one ARC-17(c) already mandates, and it is done one of two ways: strip the entry from the rendered file in post-processing, or patch the single line in the vendored copy of the library. Which was done is recorded in the technical manual. The defect has not been reported upstream, so no fixed release may be assumed: the workaround stays until somebody removes it deliberately and PLN-28's validator run still passes. | [MUST] |
| ARC-50 | **An issued document has to declare its own conformance, and a declaration needs something to declare.** Two catalogue-level entries are mandatory, and the first build of the document component was measured failing both. First, the catalogue carries an XMP metadata stream holding the PDF/UA identification schema, `pdfuaid:part` set to 1. Without it veraPDF 1.30.2 fails ISO 14289-1 clause 7.1 test 8 and rejects the file however correct its structure tree, its tagging and its text layer are; conformance that the file does not claim does not exist as far as a checker or an assistive reader is concerned. Second, `ViewerPreferences` carries `DisplayDocTitle` set to true, which is clause 7.1 test 10, **and** the document carries a real `Title` — because that entry only tells the reader to show the title in place of the file name, and a document with no title has nothing to show. The consequence for this system is concrete: a certificate is given a title naming what it is, report number and issuing unit, as part of rendering rather than as an optional flourish, and a report issued with an empty title is non-conforming. Both entries are written by the document component of ARC-17 for every document it produces, drafts included, so that the issued and the unissued paths cannot drift apart. | [MUST] |
| ARC-51 | **Every run of text declares the language it is written in, and one declaration at the top of the document is not enough.** Two separate rules apply: the natural language of the page content must be determinable, ISO 14289-1 clause 7.2 test 34, and the natural language of the text inside each `/ActualText` span must be determinable, clause 7.2 test 30. Both were measured as failures on the built component once the earlier defects were cleared, and the second is the one most easily got wrong here, because a silk testing certificate carries English, Telugu and Devanagari **on one page**. A single document-level `/Lang` cannot answer for all three: whichever value it holds, the other two scripts are mis-declared, and an assistive reader then pronounces them as that language. The rule is therefore that the catalogue carries a document `/Lang` for the prevailing language, and every marked-content span emitted under ARC-47(b) additionally carries its own `/Lang` for the run inside it. The document component enforces this at the point of the call rather than at the end of the build: it **refuses to write Indic text without an explicit language**, because a missing language is a validation failure two rules deep in a tool that runs last, and a refused call is discovered immediately by the developer who wrote it. Language is an argument to the text-drawing interface, not a template setting. | [MUST] |
| ARC-52 | **Every font program used in an issued document is embedded in it, which rules out the fonts a PDF library gives away for free.** ISO 14289-1 clause 7.21.4.1 test 1 requires embedding for every font, and the fourteen standard fonts a reader is assumed to have — Helvetica, Times, Courier and the rest — **cannot** be embedded, because a library ships their metrics and not their font programs. pdfkit draws in Helvetica unless told otherwise, so one line of Latin text set without choosing a face is enough to fail PDF/UA outright: measured, and the reason a document whose Indic handling was already faultless still failed. Latin text needs a vendored face on exactly the same footing as Telugu and Devanagari, which is why Noto Sans has been vendored for it under ARC-48. The rule for the code follows from that and is worth stating plainly, because the failure is silent at the point it is caused: the document component never relies on a default font, sets an embedded face explicitly for every run it draws, and treats an unregistered face as an error rather than falling back to one. Numerals, punctuation, the English half of a bilingual certificate and the signature block are all covered by this. | [MUST] |
| ARC-53 | **Conformance is asserted on the file the customer actually receives, which is the signed one.** A signature is applied as an incremental update — the original bytes are kept and a further revision is appended — so a validator run made before signing says nothing about the document that leaves the laboratory. The acceptance test of PLN-28 therefore validates twice, once unsigned and once after the same file has been signed, and both runs must pass with no failed rule. Measured on the built component, both do: 106 of 106 rules, reported compliant, unsigned and signed alike. The validator is **veraPDF 1.30.2, profile ua1**, pinned and named beside the test as ARC-30 requires. It is a Java program and needs Java 11 or later, and that runtime is a **build-machine dependency only**: it is never installed on the laboratory server, never invoked when a report is issued, and therefore does not enlarge the offline dependency tree that ARC-16 governs. That last point is recorded here deliberately, because the next person to read ARC-16 will otherwise assume a Java runtime has to be vendored for the unit, and it does not. | [MUST] |

#### 24.5 The public verification service — why it is separate

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-18 | The public verification service is a **separate deployment** with its own small internet-facing host, its own database containing only published verification records, and no network route back into the laboratory network. | [MUST] |
| ARC-19 | Data flows **one way only**: the laboratory server pushes a verification record outward through the queue. The public service can never write to, read from, or reach the laboratory database. | [MUST] |
| ARC-20 | The published verification record contains only: report number, report date, issuing unit, sample description, method or standard reference, live status (valid, superseded, withdrawn — the states behind the NFR-69 banner wording) with the superseding report number where applicable, the report file fingerprint, an **opaque customer token** (never a name), and optionally the headline grade if the unit enables it. | [MUST] |
| ARC-21 | The public service is read-only for the public, has no login, no administration interface reachable from the internet, no file upload that is stored, and no data-changing endpoint. The only interactive control is a file-check that hashes the visitor's own copy of the PDF **in their browser** and compares fingerprints. | [MUST] |
| ARC-22 | The public service is rate-limited per source address, does not accept a bare report number as a look-up key without the signed payload, and answers "not found" and "exists but not visible" identically so the laboratory's customer base cannot be enumerated. Burst querying raises an alert. | [MUST] |

**Why this separation matters, in one paragraph the scientist should read.** The verification page is the only part of this system that strangers can reach. If it sits on the same machine as the laboratory's records, then every weakness in that page is a route to every customer's results, every price, and every telephone number. By putting it on its own small machine that holds nothing except "report number X is valid, and here is its fingerprint", the worst that a successful attack on the public page can achieve is to learn things that are already printed on certificates people are carrying around the market. It also means the verification page keeps answering when the laboratory's power is off, and that the security audit needed before a Government-domain page goes live covers one small page instead of the whole system.

#### 24.6 Environments

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-23 | Three environments exist: **development** (the developer's machine), **staging / user acceptance testing** (a separate database and separate file storage, ideally a second physical or virtual machine at the unit), and **production**. | [MUST] |
| ARC-24 | Staging is where the laboratory does acceptance testing, and it runs on **realistic-looking but not real** data: the synthetic 5-year dataset of NFR-21, plus a set of about 50 records copied from real history with customer names, addresses and telephone numbers replaced by generated equivalents. Real production personal data is never restored into staging or development. | [MUST] |
| ARC-25 | Every release is installed on staging and accepted there before production. Monthly restore tests (NFR-99) restore into staging, which means the restore procedure is exercised as a by-product of normal work. | [MUST] |
| ARC-26 | The staging environment uses a **clearly different colour banner and the word STAGING on every screen**, and its documents are watermarked, so nobody ever mistakes a staging report for a real one. | [MUST] |
| ARC-27 | Staging uses separate test credentials for every external service, and a separate **test signing key** with its own key identifier, so a staging report can never be verified as genuine by the public service. | [MUST] |

#### 24.7 Source control, migrations, build and release — sized for one developer

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-28 | All code, database migration scripts, configuration templates, documentation and the automated test suite are in one Git repository. The repository is mirrored to a second location and handed over to Central Silk Board per NFR-113. | [MUST] |
| ARC-29 | Every database change is a **numbered, forward-only migration script** committed with the code that needs it. No change is ever made directly to a production database schema by hand. Each migration is tested by running it against a copy of production data. | [MUST] |
| ARC-30 | Continuous integration, kept deliberately simple: on every push, run the automated tests, run the dependency vulnerability scan, run the secret scanner, and produce a single deployable artefact with a version number. The document acceptance test of PLN-28 runs in that same job from the day the document component exists — PDF/UA validation of a generated report, the extracted Indic text compared character for character against the logical strings that went in, and the shaping golden file — because each defect it catches is invisible to a person reading the output, and the middle one is invisible to every validator as well. No report template is merged on the strength of a visual check. | [MUST] |
| ARC-31 | Release process, five steps, written down: (1) tag a version; (2) deploy to staging and run migrations; (3) run the automated tests and the calculation regression suite; (4) the Unit Incharge accepts on staging and signs the change record; (5) deploy to production inside the maintenance window of NFR-25, with a **written rollback step** and a database backup taken immediately before. | [MUST] |
| ARC-32 | Versions are visible: the exact version number and build date appear in the application footer and in the administrator screen, so a support question can always be answered with certainty. | [MUST] |

#### 24.8 Logging and monitoring

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-33 | An uptime check runs from outside the laboratory, every 5 minutes, against both the internal system (through whatever route exists) and the public verification service, and sends an SMS or email alert to the developer and the Unit Incharge after two consecutive failures. | [MUST] |
| ARC-34 | Unhandled errors are captured with enough context to diagnose them — the action, the user identifier, the time, the technical detail — and **with personal data removed** (NFR-57). Errors are alerted to the developer, not silently written to a file nobody reads. | [MUST] |
| ARC-35 | A simple daily health digest is emailed to the Unit Incharge and the developer: backup succeeded or failed, outbound queue depth and oldest waiting item, disk use percentage, failed logins, restore-test due date, calibrations due in the next 30 days, and the count of overdue tests. | [SHOULD] |
| ARC-36 | Application logs are separated into **audit records** (permanent, in the database, per §25), **security and access logs** (180 days, per NFR-57), and **debug logs** (14 days, freely rotated). Only the first two are protected from deletion. | [MUST] |
| ARC-37 | Every scheduled job records that it ran, when, for how long, and its outcome. A job that has not run when expected raises an alert. Silent failure of a scheduled job is the most common cause of a system that appears fine and is not. | [MUST] |

#### 24.9 Secrets and signing-key management

| ID | Requirement | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| ARC-38 | **The private signing key never leaves the server.** It is not in the repository, not in a configuration file under version control, not in an environment-variable dump, not in a database backup, and not emailed. It lives in the operating-system key store, or in a hardware security module, or in a USB hardware token in the organisation's custody. | [MUST] |
| ARC-39 | Signing is a server-side operation only. No browser, tablet or customer device ever holds or uses the key. | [MUST] |
| ARC-40 | Every signing key has a **key identifier** recorded with every document it signed, and the matching public key is published at a stable web address plus as a printable fingerprint sheet. This is what makes key rotation possible without invalidating years of already-issued reports. | [MUST] |
| ARC-41 | Key rotation is planned from the start: a documented procedure, a target rotation interval (recommended: with each certificate renewal, at least every 2 years), and the ability for the verification page to serve reports signed under **any** past key identifier. | [MUST] |
| ARC-42 | A written key-compromise procedure exists. It must include the specific behaviour that the verification page can be configured to say, for a given key identifier and date range, *"reports signed with this key require manual confirmation with the laboratory"* — rather than silently failing thousands of legitimate reports. | [MUST] |
| ARC-43 | Two key pairs exist from day one: a test key and a production key, with distinct key identifiers. A test key can never sign a production report and a production key is never present in staging or development. | [MUST] |
| ARC-44 | Application secrets (database password, SMS key, bank credentials, key passphrase) are supplied to the application by the environment or an operating-system-protected file readable only by the application account, are documented in the technical manual, and are rotatable without a code change. | [MUST] |
| ARC-45 | Signature image files, where used, are stored encrypted, readable only by their owning user's action, never applied by another user, never bulk-exportable, and every use is logged. They are never left in a shared folder — the single most common finding on this subject. | [MUST] |

#### 24.10 A plain-language note for the scientist: on-premise or cloud?

On-premise means the computer that holds your laboratory's records sits inside your building, where you can see it, and the software keeps working when the internet line fails — which at Dharmavaram it will. Cloud means those records sit in a data centre in Mumbai or Hyderabad, somebody else looks after the hardware, and you pay a monthly rent instead of buying a machine once — but when the line is down, the laboratory stops. My recommendation is the middle path: the working system lives on one small server in your laboratory, so sample login, testing, verification and report printing never depend on the internet, and only three things ever reach outside — the public report-verification page, payment confirmations from the bank, and the encrypted nightly backup. On cost, that means roughly one capital purchase of a server, a mirrored pair of disks, a third separate disk inside the server that holds nothing but the backups, one external disk that is swapped every week and taken off the premises, an uninterruptible power supply, a laser printer, a label printer and two scanners, plus a very small recurring charge for the little internet host that answers QR scans — instead of a cloud subscription that has to be sanctioned again every year. On control, it means the records are physically in Central Silk Board's custody at Dharmavaram, which is the easier position to defend to an internal auditor, to CSTRI headquarters and under the data-protection rules — and because the software is deliberately built not to depend on any one vendor, the same system can be lifted onto a Government-approved cloud later without being rewritten.

---

### 25. Database design

Naming follows the research pack: `mst_` for master (reference) data, `txn_` for transactions, `sys_` for system and platform tables. Every table has a machine-generated primary key called `id`. Human-readable numbers (sample number, report number, invoice number) are separate columns with a uniqueness rule — **never** the primary key.

Types are written in a portable form. `TIMESTAMPTZ` means "a moment in time stored in Coordinated Universal Time"; on MySQL or MariaDB use `DATETIME(3)` with the application guaranteeing UTC. `DECIMAL(p,s)` means an exact decimal number with `p` total digits and `s` after the point.

**Four columns are dormant and deliberately kept.** `mst_customer.erp_customer_id`, `mst_consumable.erp_item_id`, `mst_equipment.erp_asset_id` and `txn_invoice.erp_invoice_id` exist so that an external accounting system, if one is ever mandated, can be linked without a schema change to four large tables. While M22 is switched off — which is the only state this system is built and validated in — they are nullable, carry no foreign key and no constraint, are written by nothing and read by nothing. They are the only four: the `erp_receipt_id`, the `erp_employee_id` and the last-synchronised timestamp that M22-07 also names are **not** created now, and arrive in the migration that commissions the interface, if one ever is.

#### 25.2 Transaction tables

**The customer ledger of M17-21 is a derived view, not a table:** it is `txn_invoice` (charges, credit notes and debit notes) plus `txn_receipt` (money in and, under M17-33a, money out) plus `txn_receipt_allocation` (what has been applied to what), ordered by document date. There is deliberately no stored balance column, because a stored balance and its underlying documents cannot be made to disagree if the balance is never stored.
